overview.title: Downloading and inspecting the Jena weather data
overview.main_topic: Downloading the Jena Climate CSV, reading it into lines and a header (Listing 13.1), the 15 column names and the 420,551 records, and the start of Listing 13.2, which parses the data into NumPy arrays.
overview.central_idea: The raw dataset is a CSV with a 'Date Time' column plus 14 weather quantities, one row per 10-minute timestep, 420,551 rows; it will be parsed into a temperature array (the target) and an array of features, discarding the timestamp.
overview.importance: Every model in the chapter is trained on these arrays, so understanding their layout (rows = timesteps, columns = variables, temperature at index 1 after dropping the date) prevents off-by-one and leakage mistakes later.
learning_objectives: Download and unzip the Jena dataset.
Read the CSV with plain Python and separate the header from the records.
List the 14 measured quantities and their units.
Explain why the 'Date Time' column is discarded and how the temperature target is extracted.
Know the shapes of the arrays being built: temperature (420551,) and raw_data (420551, 14).
prerequisites: The forecasting problem and dataset description (p.376)
Basic Python string handling and NumPy arrays

summary:
The page starts with two notebook shell commands: `!wget` fetches `jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip` from the Keras datasets S3 bucket and `!unzip` extracts the CSV.

**Listing 13.1** inspects the data with plain Python: open `jena_climate_2009_2016.csv`, read the whole file into a string, split it into lines on `"\n"`, split the first line on commas to get the **header**, keep the remaining lines as data, and print the header and the number of lines.

The output is **420,551 lines** — each line is one **timestep**: a date plus **14 weather-related values** — and a header with 15 names: `"Date Time"`, `"p (mbar)"` (pressure), `"T (degC)"` (temperature), `"Tpot (K)"` (potential temperature), `"Tdew (degC)"` (dew point), `"rh (%)"` (relative humidity), `"VPmax (mbar)"`, `"VPact (mbar)"`, `"VPdef (mbar)"` (saturation, actual and deficit vapour pressure), `"sh (g/kg)"` (specific humidity), `"H2OC (mmol/mol)"` (water vapour concentration), `"rho (g/m**3)"` (air density), `"wv (m/s)"` and `"max. wv (m/s)"` (wind speed and maximum wind speed), and `"wd (deg)"` (wind direction). (The expansions of the abbreviations are ours; the page shows only the names.)

Next, all 420,551 lines are to be converted into **NumPy arrays**: one for the **temperature in degrees Celsius** (the target), and one for 'the rest of the data' — the features used to predict future temperatures. The **"Date Time" column is discarded**. **Listing 13.2** begins here with `import numpy as np` and `temperature = np.zeros((len(lines),))`; the allocation of `raw_data` and the parsing loop are on p.378 (where, note, `raw_data` keeps all 14 values, temperature included).

paragraphs.what_it_says: The lines will be converted into two NumPy arrays: one for temperature (°C), one for the rest of the data, the features used to predict future temperatures. The 'Date Time' column is discarded.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Temperature is both the target (its value 24 hours later) and, as the code on p.378 shows, also one of the input features: `raw_data` is filled with all 14 values. Using the current temperature as an input is natural (it is the strongest predictor, as the commonsense baseline on p.383 shows) and is not leakage, because the target is the temperature 24 hours later. The date is dropped because it is a string; beyond the book, calendar information (hour of day, day of year) could be encoded as features, but the periodic signals are already implicit in the measurements.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Separating the target array from the feature array makes it easy to construct (input window, future target) pairs later.

concepts.name: Jena Climate dataset
concepts.definition: Weather measurements from the Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry in Jena: 14 quantities every 10 minutes, 2009–2016 subset, 420,551 records.
concepts.intuition: Eight years of a weather station's diary, one entry every 10 minutes.
concepts.technical: CSV with columns Date Time, p (mbar), T (degC), Tpot (K), Tdew (degC), rh (%), VPmax, VPact, VPdef (mbar), sh (g/kg), H2OC (mmol/mol), rho (g/m**3), wv (m/s), max. wv (m/s), wd (deg).
concepts.example: Column index 1 after dropping the date is temperature in °C.
concepts.misconception: That the data is hourly; it is 10-minutely and will be subsampled.

concepts.name: Multivariate timeseries array layout
concepts.definition: A 2D array with time along the first axis and variables along the second.
concepts.intuition: A spreadsheet where each row is a moment and each column a sensor.
concepts.technical: Here raw_data has shape (420551, 14) and temperature shape (420551,).
concepts.significance: Standard input layout for windowed dataset utilities and sequence models.
concepts.misconception: That each row is an independent sample; consecutive rows are highly correlated and samples will be overlapping windows of rows (p.380).

code.title: Inspecting the data of the Jena weather dataset
code.original_code:
import os

fname = os.path.join("jena_climate_2009_2016.csv")

with open(fname) as f:
    data = f.read()

lines = data.split("\n")
header = lines[0].split(",")
lines = lines[1:]
print(header)
print(len(lines))
code.what_it_does: Reads the CSV into memory, separates the header row from the data rows, and prints the column names and the number of data rows.

line_explanations.explanation: Build the file path (os.path.join with a single argument just returns it; useful if you add a directory).
Read the entire file as one string (a few tens of MB, fine in memory).
Split into lines on newline characters.
First line → list of 15 column names.
Print the header (shown on the page) and 420551.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the CSV file. Output: `header` (list of 15 strings), `lines` (list of 420,551 strings).
code.algorithm: Plain-text CSV parsing without a library.
pitfalls: If the file ended with a trailing newline, split("\n") would produce an empty last string that breaks float parsing later; the count of 420,551 shows the book's file does not.
Windows line endings (\r\n) would leave \r on the last field; float() tolerates it, but string comparisons would not.

code.original_code:

The rest of Listing 13.2 is on p.378: `raw_data = np.zeros((len(lines), len(header) - 1))` and a loop that parses each line's 14 values with float(), storing values[1] in temperature[i] and all values in raw_data[i, :].

code.algorithm: Preallocate, then fill in a loop (on p.378).
pitfalls: Preallocating is much faster than appending to a Python list and converting at the end, but either works at this size.

raw_data = np.array([[float(x) for x in line.split(",")[1:]] for line in lines])

deeper.title: Sanity-checking the record count
deeper.body: 420,551 records × 10 minutes = 4,205,510 minutes = 70,091.8 hours ≈ 2,920.5 days ≈ 8.0 years — exactly the 2009–2016 span stated on p.376. A check like this quickly catches truncated downloads or a wrong sampling-rate assumption. (Our arithmetic.)

deeper.title: Is using temperature as an input feature leakage?
deeper.body:
1. The target for a window ending at time $t$ is the temperature at $t + 24$ h (p.381).
2. The inputs are measurements up to time $t$, including temperature at times $\le t$.
3. Nothing from after $t$ enters the inputs, so there is no leakage.
4. In fact the current temperature is the best single predictor: the commonsense baseline 'tomorrow = now' reaches a validation MAE of 2.44 °C (p.384).

This is why including temperature in `raw_data` (p.378) is fine even though the text on this page calls it 'the rest of the data'.

takeaways: The Jena CSV has a Date Time column plus 14 weather quantities; 420,551 data rows, one per 10 minutes over 8 years.
Listing 13.1 reads it with plain Python: split lines, split the header, drop it from the data.
The date is discarded; temperature (°C, index 1 after dropping the date) becomes the target array.
Listing 13.2 starts by preallocating temperature with np.zeros((len(lines),)); the rest is on p.378.
The code keeps temperature among the features as well, which is legitimate because the target lies 24 hours in the future.

questions.question: How many data lines does the Jena CSV contain, and what does each line represent?
questions.answer: 420,551; each line is a timestep: a date and 14 weather-related values.

questions.question: After discarding the 'Date Time' field, at which index is the temperature in °C?
questions.explanation: The header is Date Time, p (mbar), T (degC), …; dropping the first field puts p at index 0 and T at index 1 (matching temperature[i] = values[1] on p.378). Index 2 would be Tpot (K); 13 is wd (deg).

questions.question: Check that 420,551 records at 10-minute intervals cover about 8 years.
questions.explanation: Divide by 60 for hours (≈ 70,092) and by 24 for days (≈ 2,920.5); divide by 365.25 → ≈ 8.0 years, matching 2009–2016.

questions.question: The text says the second array holds 'the rest of the data', but raw_data (p.378) includes the temperature column too. Why is that not a problem for forecasting?
questions.answer: The target is the temperature 24 hours after the end of the input window, so using past and current temperatures as inputs does not leak the future; current temperature is in fact a strong predictor.
questions.explanation: Leakage would occur only if information from after the prediction time entered the inputs.

questions.question: What does `lines = lines[1:]` do in Listing 13.1?
options: Removes the header line so only data remains
questions.answer: Removes the header line so only data remains
questions.explanation: The header was already parsed from lines[0]; slicing from 1 keeps data rows. The Date Time column is dropped later, during parsing (split(",")[1:] on p.378).
